title: Building it properly: the day book

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace folder. Build the day book step by step with build.sh, then run it.

tasks.title: Load the day
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/daybook.cpp`, write `DayBook::load`, as `daybook.h` declares it: `int load(std::istream& in)`. It reads the day's file from the stream. The first line is a heading, which it skips, and so is every line that is empty or only blanks. Every other line that `parseRepair` takes is added to the book's repairs, in order. It gives back how many lines it refused. `repair.h` declares `parseRepair`, and `trim` from this part's third issue too, so `daybook.cpp` can call both.

Check compiles `daybook.cpp` and `repair.cpp` each on its own, with `-std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra`, and links them with a program of its own, which makes a `DayBook`, hands `load` string streams of its own and reads the book back through `all()`. A warning in your lines fails the task.
nextSteps: Write the first line, with `DayBook::` in front of `load`, exactly as `daybook.h` declares it.
Read the stream a line at a time, counting the lines.
Skip the heading and every blank line.
Hand every other line to `parseRepair`: keep the repair in `repairs`, or count the line as refused.
hints: This is last issue's reading of the day, inside a class this time: the member `repairs` is the list it fills.

A member function written below its class has the class's name and `::` in front of its own name, and its first line matches the declaration in the header exactly. A blank line of a Windows file still holds a carriage return, so ask whether it is empty once it is trimmed.

The shape is `int DayBook::load(std::istream& in) { std::string line; int number = 0; int refused = 0; while (std::getline(in, line)) { number++; if (number == 1 || trim(line).empty()) { continue; } Repair repair; if (parseRepair(line, repair)) { repairs.push_back(repair); } else { refused++; } } return refused; }`.

tasks.title: Find the longest repair
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2` in `src/daybook.cpp`, write `DayBook::longest`, as `daybook.h` declares it: `const Repair* longest() const`, with `std::max_element`. It gives back the address of the repair in the book with the most minutes, the first of them when several have as many, or `nullptr` when the book is empty.

Check builds this task with a `load` of its own in place of yours, written as Task 1 asks. It fills books of its own, with two repairs of the most minutes in one and nothing in another, and looks at where the address `longest` gives back points: at which repair of the book, or nowhere. A warning in your lines fails the task.
nextSteps: Write the first line, with `DayBook::` in front and `const` at the end, as the header declares it.
Give back `nullptr` for an empty book.
Hand `std::max_element` the repairs and a comparison of their minutes, and give back the address of what it finds.
hints: Part 8 handed the algorithms a rule. `std::max_element` gives back an iterator to the largest item, by the rule it is handed: whether the first of two items comes before the second.

On an empty range it gives back the end, which is no item at all. Of equal ones it keeps the first, as long as the rule says strictly fewer. `&*` turns an iterator into the address of the item it points at.

The shape is `if (repairs.empty()) { return nullptr; } auto found = std::max_element(repairs.begin(), repairs.end(), [](const Repair& a, const Repair& b) { return a.minutes < b.minutes; }); return &*found;`.

tasks.title: Declare and write the summary
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3` in `src/report.h`, declare a function called `writeSummary` that takes a stream as a reference to a `std::ostream` and the day book as a reference to a `const DayBook`, and gives nothing back. Under `// Task 3` in `src/report.cpp`, write it. It writes three lines, each with its line end:

```
Repairs: 4
Minutes: 240
Longest: ticket 3201, 75 minutes
```

with how many repairs the book holds, all their minutes, and the ticket and minutes of the repair `longest` gives back, or `Longest: none` when the book is empty.

Check compiles `report.cpp` on its own and links it with a program of its own that includes `report.h`, with a `DayBook` of its own written as Tasks 1 and 2 ask. It hands `writeSummary` a string stream and books of its own, an empty one among them. A warning in your lines fails the task.
nextSteps: In `report.h`, under `// Task 3`, write the first line of `writeSummary`, with a semicolon in place of its body.
In `report.cpp`, write the same first line again, with its body.
Write the first two lines from what the book can tell you.
Ask `longest` for the longest repair, and look at what it gives back before you use it.
hints: Part 4 split a function this way: a header declares it, so every file that includes the header can call it, and one `.cpp` file writes its body.
The book is `const` here, and every member function it offers is `const` too. `longest` gives back a pointer, which is `nullptr` for an empty book: reading through it then stops the program.

The shape is `void writeSummary(std::ostream& out, const DayBook& book);` in the header, and in `report.cpp` a body that writes `book.count()` and `book.totalMinutes()`, then `const Repair* longest = book.longest();` and an `if` on `longest == nullptr`.

tasks.title: Compile the other files, then link
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4` in `build.sh`, write one line for each of the other three `.cpp` files in `src`, like the line given for `repair.cpp`: compiled on its own with `$FLAGS` and `-c`, into its own `.o` file in `build`. Then write one line, after them, that links every `.o` file into the program `daybook`, in the workspace folder.

Check does not run `build.sh`. It reads it as `sh` would and looks at what each `g++` line would do: that every `.cpp` file of `src` is compiled once, on a line of its own, with `-c`, `-std=c++17`, `-Wall` and `-Wextra`, into an object file, with paths written from the workspace folder; that no header is compiled; and that one line after them, without `-c`, links every one of those object files and no `.cpp` file into `daybook`. The order of the files on a line and of the flags does not matter, and the given lines stay as they are.
nextSteps: Read the given line for `repair.cpp`: the flags, `-c`, the file, and `-o` with the object file.
Write a line like it for `daybook.cpp`, `report.cpp` and `main.cpp`.
Write the link line: every object file, then `-o daybook`.
Run `sh build.sh && ./daybook`, change one `.cpp` file, and run it again.
hints: Each `.cpp` file becomes an object file on its own line, and only the link line joins them. The flags that say how code is read go where the code is read.
A path in `build.sh` is read from the workspace folder: its `cd` line moves there first, wherever it is run from. The link line hands the compiler object files only, so nothing is compiled twice.
The lines are `g++ $FLAGS -c src/daybook.cpp -o build/daybook.o`, the same for `report.cpp` and `main.cpp`, and then `g++ build/repair.o build/daybook.o build/report.o build/main.o -o daybook`.
